questions.prompt: What privilege level is required to begin a Kerberoasting attack?
options: Any authenticated domain user -- requesting a service ticket for an SPN is an ordinary operation
Local administrator on a domain controller
Replication rights on the domain object
questions.explanation: Requesting a service ticket for any SPN is a normal Kerberos operation available to any authenticated domain user, which is precisely why Kerberoasting is so commonly observed.

questions.prompt: Why is the cracking phase of Kerberoasting invisible to domain defenses?
options: Because the domain controller suppresses those logs by default
Because it happens offline on the attacker's own hardware -- no rate limit, no account lockout, and no logging apply
Because Kerberos does not log service ticket requests
Because the tickets are deleted immediately after issuance
questions.explanation: Once the ticket is obtained, password guessing happens entirely off-network against the attacker's own copy, where none of the domain's protective controls have any visibility or effect.

questions.prompt: Why do attacker tools frequently request RC4-encrypted tickets even in AES environments?
options: RC4 is the only encryption Kerberos supports for service tickets
RC4-encrypted tickets crack dramatically faster than AES, making the downgrade request itself a useful detection signal
AES tickets cannot be extracted from memory
RC4 requests bypass Event ID 4769 logging entirely
questions.explanation: The downgrade to RC4 speeds up offline cracking substantially. In an environment standardized on AES, an RC4 ticket request stands out as a strong indicator.

questions.prompt: Why do Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) effectively neutralize Kerberoasting?
options: They prevent service tickets from being issued at all
They use automatically-managed 240-character passwords that rotate on a schedule, making offline cracking computationally infeasible
They remove the SPN from the account automatically
They encrypt tickets with a key the KDC never sees
questions.explanation: The attack still technically works -- a ticket can still be requested -- but the resulting hash is derived from a 240-character machine-generated password, removing any realistic chance of cracking it.
